newsitem.title: USA: Rich, famous live in denial about security threat.
newsitem.headline: Rich, famous live in denial about security threat.

text.p: While many stars live behind the walls of gated estates and hire burly bodyguards, others put themselves in the path of danger by refusing to acknowledge that fame has its risks, security experts say.

Since the death of ex-Beatle John Lennon, slain by a stalker on the sidewalk outside his New York apartment building in 1980, the protection of the rich and famous has become a growth industry in the United States.
Yet, as the broad daylight murder of Italian fashion designer Gianni Versace shows, celebrities create risk by refusing to take seriously the fact that their renown makes them targets, experts said.
Versace, 50, was shot twice in the head on Tuesday on the steps of his Spanish-style mansion on Ocean Drive as he strolled home from a cafe after picking up magazines.
An alleged "spree killer" and homosexual prostitute, Andrew Cunanan, is suspected of gunning down the glamorous designer who dressed the world's rich and famous.
"The most difficult person to sell security to is the celebrity," Tom Cash, a security consultant with Kroll Associates, a Miami security firm, said.

In Los Angeles and elsewhere, security firms are doing a booming trade protecting the captains of industry and entertainment. Versace's death had resulted in more inquiries about personal security, several security companies said.
"It's a big business. It's getting bigger," said Drew Levine, South Florida vice president of Wackenhut Corp, a major security firm.
The threat of stalkers led the police department in Los Angeles, home to the world's biggest gallery of stars, to form a Threat Management Unit, or anti-stalker squad.

Most U.S. states now have stalking laws, spurred to action by the 1989 murder of rising Hollywood actress Rebecca Schaeffer by a fan who hired a detective to find her home address. The fan then knocked on her door and shot her dead.
In May 1995, a private security guard shot an intruder at Madonna's Hollywood Hills home.
In July 1996, a security guard at the Miami waterfront estate of actor Sylvester Stallone hacked another guard with a knife during a robbery attempt.
The Versace slaying has stirred more outrage than fear in the modelling world, said Jessica Aufiero, spokeswoman for Elite Model Management in New York.
"The girls, if they want to have bodyguards, it's sort of up to them. Models like Claudia Schiffer or Linda Evangelista, it would be at their discretion," she said.

Levine described security as a classic catch-22 for celebrities. "They've worked their entire careers to get to the position they're in," he said. "But the drawback to that is that they can't go out in public."

According to Cash, the main challenge in protecting celebrities is persuading them they need it. "Many celebrities refuse to believe they're at risk," he said. "They have a tendency to be amazed at their own fame."
Cash said many burdened by the "albatross of celebrity" lived in a state of denial, believing they were simply "ordinary folks with jobs that pay really well."
While money and sex are a motive for many crimes, fame is at the heart of celebrity stalking, Cash said.
"It's fixation more than money and sex. The self-aggrandizement of the shooter," he said. "People who do these shootings are generally trying to achieve notoriety."
Often, celebrities are forewarned, through letters or phone calls from the stalker, and choose to ignore the threat.
"Many just reject these warnings out of hand," Cash said. "There should always be a studious review, not just an 'in the garbage can' rejection of letters."

While stars are well protected at concerts, fashion shows and movie openings, they are most vulnerable while travelling or simply "moving through the world," experts said. Security ultimately can be a lifestyle choice, and in Versace's case he chose to revel in the freedom of the common man.
"He wanted to be a regular guy who walked down the street to get his own coffee," Levine said.
